1.goal: To open the lesson on a conversation she knows from work, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she gives feedback to a teacher she observed, and keeps it when he disagrees.
Ask the question on screen and take one short answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you give feedback to a teacher you observed. Then you give it again, and he does not agree.”
1.expected: A short answer about when and to whom, for example “Last month, to a new teacher, after I watched his class.”
1.support: If she has not given feedback in English, ask about the last time in Portuguese.
1.monitoring: Whether she has a real conversation to draw on.
1.transition: Move on as soon as she has answered.

2.goal: To establish her role, the teacher's position, what she saw, and what she wants from the conversation.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “One thing he will try this week, and that he chose it.” The brief gives it in the last line. The case is fictional; if she asks, confirm it.
2.support: If she answers with what she wants to tell him, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what changes in the conversation because he is not obliged to accept anything.
2.monitoring: Whether she notices that the result has to be his choice.
2.evidence: Whether she can say the goal of the conversation without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she has said what she wants him to leave with.

3.goal: To hear the feedback she gives today, before any model.
3.interaction: Role-play. You are the teacher she observed, and you say very little.
run: Read the task and the three questions with her.
Listen. A short “right” or “OK” is enough; let the feedback be as long or as short as it comes.
Leave corrections for screen 10. Write down her recommendation word for word: it goes into the third box on screen 10.
exact: If she stops after the observation: “And what would you suggest?”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: it is the version she already has. What usually comes: the observation said clearly, and the recommendation said as an instruction, for example “You have to give the instruction before they start.”
3.support: If she stops, ask the question in the note, and nothing more.
3.challenge: None on this screen. What she says here is compared with screen 8.
3.monitoring: Where the observation ends and the recommendation starts, and what form the recommendation takes.
3.transition: Move on when she has given the feedback once.

4.goal: To hear one model of the same feedback, and to find where it leaves the teacher room to answer.
run: Play the five lines one at a time.
After each line, ask the question below.
Then ask the question on screen.
exact: After each line: “What can he say back to that?”
If she answers “nothing”: “Then who decides what happens next?”
4.expected: The observation comes first (“What I noticed was the instruction coming while they were still working.”), then a real question (“What were you trying to do at that point?”). The teacher can say no to the recommendation and still be talking about the same thing at “One thing you might try is giving the instruction before they start…” and at “I might be wrong about the reason.”
4.support: Play the recommendation line again, and ask whether it is an order or an option.
4.challenge: Ask which line she would find hardest to say to a teacher she does not know.
4.monitoring: Whether she notices that the recommendation is offered, not given as an order.
4.evidence: The lines she chooses as the ones he could answer.
4.transition: Move on when she has found where he could say no.

5.goal: To sort six recommendations by whether they leave the teacher room to answer.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her place the six and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each, ask what the teacher could say back.
Leave the discussion of the polite one for the next screen.
5.expected: he can answer it: “One thing you might try is giving it before they start.” · “Have you thought about giving it before they start?” · “It might be worth trying it before they start -- what do you think?” he can only accept it: “You have to give the instruction before they start.” · “Please give the instruction first next time.” · “The instruction needs to come first.”
5.support: On each one, ask: after this sentence, can he say “no, because…” and still be in the conversation?
5.challenge: Ask her to turn “The instruction needs to come first.” into one he can answer.
5.monitoring: Whether she places “Please give the instruction first next time.” with the ones he can answer. It is polite, and it is still an order.
5.evidence: Which ones she placed with the answerable group at first.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed.

6.goal: To have her explain why a polite order is still an order, and to hear the forms that leave the decision with him.
run: Read the question and the sentence with her.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open the reveal and read it with her. Then ask her to say the same point in one of the three forms.
exact: If she says “because it is polite”: “Polite, yes. After it, what can he answer?”
6.expected: Please softens the order, but it gives him nothing to answer: the decision is still hers. From the reveal: “One thing you might try…” gives him one option among others; “Have you thought about…?” is a question, so he can answer; “It might be worth… — what do you think?” hands him the decision in words.
6.support: Ask her to imagine answering the sentence as the teacher: what would she say?
6.challenge: Ask for a fourth form that leaves the decision with him.
6.monitoring: Whether she separates politeness from leaving room to answer.
6.evidence: The form she chooses for her own version.
6.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has said her own version.

7.goal: To say the recommendation in four forms that leave the decision with him, before the conversation.
7.interaction: S alone on the gap-fill, then T–S, spoken.
run: Let her complete the four sentences and press Check.
Ask her to say each one to you out loud, as if you were the teacher.
After each one, answer briefly as the teacher, so she hears that he can answer.
exact: Answering as the teacher: “Maybe. I would need to see how long it takes.”
7.expected: “One thing you might try is giving it before they start.” · “Have you thought about repeating it after they begin?” · “It might be worth checking with the two slower pairs.” · “I might be wrong about the reason — what I saw was the pattern.”
7.support: If she reads the sentences flat, say one with a falling tone on might and let her repeat it.
7.challenge: Ask her to add a reason from what she saw to one of the four.
7.monitoring: The tone of might: falling, it is a suggestion; rising, it sounds like asking permission.
7.evidence: Which forms she says without reading.
7.transition: Move on when the four have been said out loud.

8.goal: To give the whole feedback, round one, choosing what she gives feedback on, with the sentence starters closed.
8.interaction: Role-play, round one. You are the teacher, and in this round you listen and accept.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose one.
Let her open and run the feedback. Answer her question about what you were trying to do.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, and close them again. Leave corrections for screen 10.
Write down her recommendation as she said it.
exact: If she asks what you were trying to do (option A): “I wanted to save time. The next task is long.”
If she asks what you were trying to do (option B): “I wanted to check they understood, and the first answer was right.”
8.expected: The four things on the list, for the option she chose. For option A, something like “What I noticed was that the instruction came while the pairs were still working. What were you trying to do at that point? … One thing you might try is giving it before they start. I might be wrong about the reason.” For option B, the same shape about the checking question: “What I noticed was that three hands were still up when you moved on.”
8.support: If the recommendation comes out as an order, leave it and note it for screen 10.
8.challenge: Ask her to use your answer about what you were trying to do in her recommendation.
8.monitoring: The form of the recommendation, compared with the one she said on screen 3.
8.evidence: The option she chose and her recommendation, word for word.
8.transition: Move on when she has given the recommendation.

9.goal: To keep the conversation going after the feedback: answer two questions from the teacher with what she saw, and ask one back.
9.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the teacher.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
After each answer, wait.
Then ask her to put one question to you and to agree with you on one thing to try.
exact: Question 1: “Right. Which part of the lesson was that?”
Question 2: “And what were the others doing while that happened?”
Handing the turn over: “OK. Anything else?”
9.expected: Two answers with what she saw, and a question from her. For option A: “It was the error task, when you gave the next instruction.” and “Two pairs were still writing.” For option B: “It was the checking question at the end.” and “Three of them still had their hands up.” Her question can be “Is there anything you would like me to look at next time?”, and the close names one thing he will try.
9.support: If the second answer comes as a judgment (“they were lost”), ask “What did you see them doing?”.
9.challenge: Ask “So what do you want me to do?” and let her keep the decision with you.
9.monitoring: Whether her answers stay with what she saw, and whether she hands the decision back.
9.evidence: Whether she asked a question of her own, and what you agreed he would try.
9.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and the conversation has closed on something to try.

10.goal: To put her first and second recommendations side by side, and to build the sentence she uses in round two.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve.
Write her recommendation from screen 3 in the third box, word for word, and ask her to write the version from screen 8, or a clearer one, in the fourth.
Ask her which of the two he could answer, and why.
10.expected: Two versions of the recommendation. If they are different — for example “You have to give the instruction before they start.” and “One thing you might try is giving it before they start.” — say the difference out loud. If they are the same, that goes in the record too.
10.support: If she cannot see the difference, read the two out loud and ask which one he could say no to.
10.challenge: Ask for the fourth-box sentence with the observation attached, in one turn.
10.monitoring: Whether the second version leaves the decision with him.
10.evidence: The two versions and the one she chooses for round two.
10.transition: Move on when the sentence for round two has been said once.

11.goal: To give the same feedback again under a new condition: the teacher disagrees, and he is partly right.
11.interaction: Role-play, round two. You are the teacher, and this time you disagree.
run: Let her open the same way.
When she gets to the recommendation, disagree with the first line below for her option. If she holds the point, use the second.
Disagree with an argument, not with hostility. He is partly right, and that is the point.
The sentence starters stay closed until she stops.
exact: Option A, first: “I did give it before they started. I said it twice, actually. They were not listening.”
Option B, first: “I did check. I asked a question, and the answer was right.”
Second, for either: “So you are saying it is my teaching, and I am saying it is their attention.”
11.expected: She says what is right in his answer and keeps what she saw. A complete answer sounds like “That is fair, you did say it twice. The part I would still look at is that two pairs were still writing when it came.” — the concession, and the observation kept.
11.support: If the recommendation disappears, ask “What is still true after what I said?” and wait.
11.challenge: Add a second objection about the slower pairs and see whether the observation still stands.
11.monitoring: Whether she concedes and holds, concedes and drops the point, or does not concede at all. Only the first is the target.
11.evidence: What of her feedback was still there after the disagreement.
11.transition: Move on when she has answered the objection and the conversation has closed.

12.goal: To close the lesson and the block: what was worked on, how confident she feels, and the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “In your next feedback conversation, say one recommendation so the teacher can answer it.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: opening with what she saw, a recommendation he can answer, saying where she might be wrong, asking what he was trying to do, answering his questions with what she saw, keeping the recommendation when he disagreed, and closing with something he can try. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, read her two versions from screen 10 back to her.
12.challenge: Ask when her next real feedback conversation is.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and the date of her next feedback conversation if she has one.
12.transition: End here. This lesson closes the block.
